newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - WHSmith under pressure as CEO quits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - WHSmith under pressure as CEO quits.

text.p: W.H. Smith Group Plc's shares fell steeply on Monday after the British retailing group stunned investors with news that chief executive Bill Cockburn was quitting to join British Telecom.

Smith, which posted its first loss in more than 200 years last summer, saw its shares drop nearly 10 percent after the announcement of Cockburn's departure. They stood 35 pence lower at 376-1/2 pence.
Cockburn, who joined Smith just eighteen months ago, will be leaving the group in the middle of a campaign to revitalise its core chain.

The stores, on nearly every main shopping street around the country, have been struggling to combat increasingly cut-throat competition from margin-hungry food superstores such as ASDA Group Plc and Tesco Plc, which have muscled in on its traditional market for newspapers, books and videos.

Cockburn was brought in in November 1995 to shake up the family business and find a way to secure the future of the W.H.Smith chain. His departure inevitably increased uncertainty about Smith's prospects, analysts said.
"He was the driving force behind strategic moves at W.H. Smith (retail)," said one analyst, who asked not to be identified. "Investors will be unsure now what the strategy will be going forward."

Chairman Jeremy Hardie said that Cockburn had been a catalyst for change within the group, presiding over the sale of several of Smith's non-core businesses, notably Do It All home improvement stores and Business Supplies.
Cockburn said in the statement, "Normally I would have wanted to see my plans through to fruition. My decision to join BT was not taken lightly but it is the chance of a lifetime for me."
Hardie told Reuters in a telephone interview the chief executive's departure had nothing to do with problems at the retailing group.
He said Cockburn, who will leave Smith's in October, had received an "irresistible" offer from BT and his decision to leave did not reflect any difficulties at W.H.Smith.
"It's not to do with any problems, it's to do with an irresistible offer," Hardie said.
Cockburn also told Reuters the decision to leave was "all to do with this glittering opportunity at BT and mustn't be interpreted that there are problems here."
Cockburn said BT had approached him and offered the job of managing director of BT in the UK, which was too good an offer to turn down.

Cockburn, who moved to W.H.Smith the Post Office, said he would be running BT in the UK after the company completes its merger with U.S. telecoms group MCI Communications Corp . He said there was a certain irony in the BT job as he had started his working life at the company.
He said W.H. Smith's new management team, including Beverley Hodson, the newly appointed managing director of the core retail chain, were well placed to drive the business forward.
The company made a profit in the first half, but retail analysts are still worried about the long term future of the core W.H. Smith chain.

The UK food retailers' search for higher margins by selling more non-food goods has eaten away at W.H. Smith's traditional market, and analysts said Cockburn faced a tough job trying to reverse this trend.
Hardie said the group was already looking for a replacement for Cockburn, but declined to speculate on how long it might take.
"It will take a little while to find someone," said Rowan Morgan, retail analyst at Nikko Europe, "there's no obvious successor.
The drop in the shares, and management upheaval could revive speculation about a possible bid for Smiths, he said.
W.H.Smith also said its results for the year to March 31, 1997 would be within the range of market expectations, which are between 124 million and 130 million pounds ($215.1 million).
The retailer said sales in the second half were up six percent overall and ahead three percent on a comparable store basis.
Analysts said the progress in W.H. Smith retail in the second half had been slower than hoped for.
BT shares were little moved after the news, easing 1-1/2p to 447 in a generally lower London market. ($ = 0.604 British Pounds)
